passages.t: Joash repairs the house of God
passages.happening:
‘Joash was seven years old when he became king, and he reigned in Jerusalem forty years’ (verse 1). ‘And Joash did what was right in the eyes of the LORD all the days of Jehoiada the priest’ (verse 2). ‘Some time later, Joash set his heart on repairing the house of the LORD’ (verse 4). The Levites are slow to collect the money (verse 5), so he has a chest made and set outside the gate, and a proclamation calls Judah to bring ‘the tax imposed by Moses the servant of God on Israel in the wilderness’ (verse 9). ‘All the officers and all the people rejoiced and brought their contributions, and they dropped them in the chest until it was full’ (verse 10).

The workers restore the house, and the rest of the money makes vessels of gold and silver; burnt offerings are offered regularly all of Jehoiada's days (verses 12-14). ‘When Jehoiada was old and full of years, he died at the age of 130’ (verse 15). ‘And Jehoiada was buried with the kings in the City of David, because he had done what was good in Israel for God and His temple’ (verse 16).
passages.hearers:
The child who was the promise's last thread now reigns forty years, commonly placed about 835 to 796 BC, and the chapter splits his reign cleanly in two, hinged on Jehoiada's death. In the first half he repairs the house of God; in the second he abandons it.

The tax of Moses was the half-shekel for the tent of meeting, which the Chronicler presents as an annual duty for the temple. The chest at the gate made giving public, and the joint emptying by the royal scribe and the high priest's officer was a simple guard against misuse. Kings adds that the chest had a hole in its lid and stood beside the altar.

Burial with the kings was an honor, and the Chronicler gives it to the priest Jehoiada, while the king will be denied it. Who to notice: Jehoiada, whose life held the reign steady.
passages.later: The law said, ‘When you take a census of the Israelites to number them, each man must pay the LORD a ransom for his life when he is counted’ (Exodus 30:12).
passages.asks: Joash did what was right all the days of Jehoiada. Ask whose faithfulness is holding your own steady. And ask what would remain of your faith if that person were gone.

passages.t: Joash turns, and Zechariah is stoned
passages.happening:
‘After the death of Jehoiada, however, the officials of Judah came and paid homage to the king, and he listened to them’ (verse 17). ‘They abandoned the house of the LORD, the God of their fathers, and served the Asherah poles and idols’ (verse 18). ‘Nevertheless, the LORD sent prophets to bring the people back to Him and to testify against them; but they would not listen’ (verse 19).

‘Then the Spirit of God came upon Zechariah son of Jehoiada the priest’ (verse 20), and he tells the people God's word: ‘Why do you transgress the commandments of the LORD so that you cannot prosper? Because you have forsaken the LORD, He has forsaken you’ (verse 20). ‘But they conspired against Zechariah, and by order of the king, they stoned him in the courtyard of the house of the LORD’ (verse 21). ‘Thus King Joash failed to remember the kindness that Zechariah’s father Jehoiada had extended to him’ (verse 22). As he dies, Zechariah says, “May the LORD see this and call you to account” (verse 22).

In the spring a small Aramean army defeats Judah's great one (verses 23-24). Joash is left wounded, and his own servants kill him on his bed ‘for shedding the blood of the son of Jehoiada the priest’ (verse 25). He is buried in the City of David, but not in the tombs of the kings.
passages.hearers:
The second panel reverses the first. Joash did what was right in Jehoiada's days; after him the people abandoned the house of the LORD. Zechariah's message turns on one verb twice, forsake, azav, and the narrator repeats it in verse 24. Literally the Spirit of God clothed Zechariah, lavash, the same vivid image used of Gideon and Amasai.

Kings tells the chest, and an attack by Hazael of Aram that Joash bought off with temple and palace treasures. Chronicles adds Jehoiada's death, the officials' turn to idols, the prophets' warnings and the stoning of Zechariah, and reads the Aramean invasion and the assassination as their consequence. The few defeating the many reverses the earlier chapters, where a faithful Judah overcame larger forces.

Bloodshed in the temple court was desecration: the place of atonement became the place where an innocent man's blood was spilled. Zechariah asks God to see and to require an account, the old conviction that innocent blood cries out to God. The king who forgot Jehoiada's kindness, chesed, is killed for shedding the blood of Jehoiada's son, and the priest lies with the kings while the king does not.
passages.later: Jesus spoke of this murder. To the scribes and Pharisees of his day he said, ‘And so upon you will come all the righteous blood shed on earth, from the blood of righteous Abel to the blood of Zechariah son of Berechiah, whom you murdered between the temple and the altar’ (Matthew 23:35). Luke's version reads, ‘from the blood of Abel to the blood of Zechariah, who was killed between the altar and the sanctuary’ (Luke 11:51).
passages.hard:
Matthew calls the murdered Zechariah the son of Berechiah, but this chapter says he was the son of Jehoiada. Which is it? And what does Jesus' saying mean?

Matthew 23:35 names Zechariah son of Berechiah; this chapter names Zechariah son of Jehoiada; Luke gives no father's name. The prophet Zechariah of the late sixth century BC was the son of Berechiah, but the Old Testament does not tell how he died. Skeptics have long called this a plain mistake, and many scholars think Matthew, or the tradition he used, merged the two men. Others offer different explanations. Some think son of Berechiah was added by an early copyist: Jerome, writing around 398, reported that the Gospel used by a group of Jewish Christians, the Nazarenes, read son of Jehoiada here, and one major old manuscript lacks the words in its first hand. Some suggest that Jehoiada had a second name, or was Zechariah's grandfather, though there is no evidence of it. A few point to a later Zechariah murdered in the temple during the war with Rome, but most reject this, since Jesus speaks of a murder already done, and the temple court and the Abel-to-Chronicles frame point strongly to this chapter. Christians who hold a high view of Scripture are found on more than one side, and these notes do not choose.

Abel's murder is the first told in Genesis, and Zechariah's is the last told in Chronicles, the last book in the Hebrew order, so many read Jesus' words as the whole span of the Hebrew Scriptures. On every view all the righteous blood, from first to last, comes to its reckoning.

Jesus was speaking to leaders of his own day about what they themselves were about to do, and of a judgment that would fall in that generation. Scripture forbids putting the guilt of fathers on children. For centuries many Christians used scenes like this to justify contempt, expulsions and violence against Jews. That reading is false, and Christians must reject it plainly. These words give no one reason to blame the Jewish people, then or now.
passages.asks: Zechariah told the truth in the temple court and was killed there by order of a king his father had saved. Ask whose kindness to you you have forgotten. And ask whether there is a truth-teller in your life you have silenced, or would.
